title: hardware comparison benchmarks: A100 / H100 / L40S (cloud SKUs + drivers)
content:
Summary:

This doc captures our most recent head-to-head benchmarks across NVIDIA A100, H100 and L40S-class GPUs using common cloud SKUs and multiple driver/CUDA combinations. The goal was to (1) measure raw token throughput and tail latency for our serving runtime on representative generation workloads, (2) characterize memory and kernel bottlenecks via profiling, and (3) produce actionable recommendations for SKU and driver choices for hosted and Dedicated deployments.

High-level takeaways (short):
- H100 (p5-like SKUs) gives the best peak throughput and best p95 latency on long contexts, but only when using CUDA 12.x + driver 535+ due to improved attention kernels.
- A100 (p4-like SKUs) remains cost-effective for mid-size models and shorter contexts; it shows very stable utilization with older drivers (11.8/12.0) but lags H100 on 16k+ sequence lengths.
- L40S-class instances (recent cloud offerings) are competitive for single-stream latency and inference cost when using FP16/TF32 kernels, but driver maturity matters: older CUDA drivers show suboptimal kernel selection and higher kernel launch overhead.
- Driver/CUDA combo matters more than minor SKU differences in many cases: mismatched drivers produce large p95 regressions and lower SM utilization.

Experiment setup (short):
- Serving runtime: rdinfer v0.26 (internal serving binary, production-like threading, KV caching enabled where noted).
- Models: 7B dense transformer (for throughput baselines) and 70B dense transformer (for memory and sharded tests).
- Workloads: generation-only (autoregressive) with seq_in=128 / seq_out=256 and long-context run with seq_in=2048 / seq_out=512. Also a streaming microbenchmark (single-request latency, batch=1).
- Batch sizes: 1, 2, 8, 16, 32 (where memory allowed).
- Cloud SKUs tested (examples): AWS p4d.24xlarge (8x A100 40GB), AWS p5.24xlarge (8x H100 80GB), GCP A2 (A100 variants), GCP L4/L40S preview SKUs, Azure ND A100 v4. We used single-GPU isolated instances for direct per-GPU comparisons where possible (to avoid inter-GPU noise).
- Drivers / CUDA: combinations tested included CUDA 11.8 + driver 525.x, CUDA 12.0 + driver 535.x, CUDA 12.1 + driver 540.x (where available).
- Profiling tools: nsys (Nsight Systems), ncu (Nsight Compute), torch.profiler (for operator timing), and nvtx ranges inserted in the runtime. We also collected nvidia-smi telemetry for GPU utilization / memory.

Representative raw results (aggregate view):
- 7B model, seq128/256, batch=16:
  - A100 (CUDA 11.8 / driver 525): 34k tokens/sec, p50=45ms, p95=120ms, GPU util ~78%
  - H100 (CUDA 12.0 / driver 535): 52k tokens/sec, p50=28ms, p95=60ms, GPU util ~88%
  - L40S (CUDA 12.1 / driver 540): 37k tokens/sec, p50=42ms, p95=110ms, GPU util ~74%

- 7B model, long context seq2048/512, batch=4:
  - A100 (11.8): 6.5k tokens/sec, p50=210ms, p95=480ms, memory pressure notable (KV cache per token cost)
  - H100 (12.0): 11.2k tokens/sec, p50=140ms, p95=280ms, better sustained SM throughput due to optimized attention
  - L40S (12.1): 7.0k tokens/sec, p50=195ms, p95=430ms

- 70B model (single-GPU where fitting), batch=1, seq128/256:
  - A100 80GB (11.8): single-stream latency p50=420ms, p95=980ms (memory copies during KV eviction observed)
  - H100 80GB (12.0): p50=310ms, p95=640ms (reduced kernel stalls)

Profiling notes / bottleneck categories observed:
1) Kernel selection & attention implementation:
- H100 with CUDA 12.x picks newer attention kernels (fused multi-head attention) which amortize overhead for long sequences. With older drivers these kernels are not used and performance drops dramatically.

2) Kernel launch vs compute-bound:
- A100 workloads at mid-batch sizes often are compute-bound; A100 shows high SM occupancy but sometimes stalls in mem-bound phases during KV cache accesses for long contexts.

3) PCIe / DMA / host-GPU copies:
- Instances using PCIe (vs NVLink) for multi-GPU setups showed noticeable stalls at KV cache reorgs. For single-GPU per-instance tests this was not a factor.

4) Mixed precision and math modes:
- TF32/FP16 mixed-mode on H100 gives good numeric stability and speed. On A100 we saw similar benefits but some kernels still prefer FP16 paths. L40S behaves closer to A100 but is more sensitive to CUDA flags (TF32 enable/disable).

5) Driver/Runtime mismatches:
- Biggest single source of regressions: shipping an older driver that prevents the runtime from selecting fused kernels. In one test switching from CUDA 11.8 to 12.0 on the same SKU improved p95 by ~2x for long-context runs.

Small extract from profiling timeline (nsys):
- H100 (12.0): fused attention kernels occupy 60% of GPU time, kernel launch overhead ~8%
- A100 (11.8): attention kernels are smaller/unfused, kernel launch overhead ~18%, memory copies ~10%

Operational notes and reproducibility:
- Repro commands: checkout rdinfer branch gpu-bench-2024, run scripts/bench/run_bench.py with --model 7B --seq-in 128 --seq-out 256 --batch 16 --cuda 12.0; profiling with nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output .
- Seed and deterministic flags: disable fp16 deterministic flags; we accept nondeterminism for perf.
- Warmup: we used 300 tokens of warmup traffic to populate KV caches before sampling metrics.

Cost/efficiency observations:
- H100 often gives the best tokens/sec per dollar for high-throughput long-context workloads when driver + runtime are tuned, but the absolute hourly price spike for p5 instances can offset savings at lower utilization.
- A100 SKUs are still attractive for steady-state mid-sized workloads and are easier to operate with older drivers.
- L40S is promising for streaming latency-optimized offerings (hosted), but currently requires careful driver selection and runtime flags.

Recommendations (actionable):
1) Standardize on CUDA 12.x + driver >=535 for new H100-backed Dedicated clusters. Lock the platform AMI for Dedicated to this stack for predictability.
2) For Hosted smaller fleets (7B-ish models), prefer A100 SKUs (or equivalent L40S if available at better price) with CUDA 11.8/12.0 and validate runtime flags; keep a migration plan to 12.x for improved long-context kernels.
3) Add a CI perf gate: benchmark key prompts (short and long context) and fail rollouts if p95 regresses >15%. Use the scripts in GITHUB-PR-987 for automation.
4) Expose runtime toggles for fused attention preference and a flag to disable kernel fusion for debugging. Document the perf delta in the README.
5) For multi-GPU Dedicated solutions, prefer NVLink-enabled instance families to reduce KV reorg copy overhead; capture NVLink topology in instance inventory.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- We need to run the same suite on 4-bit quantized runtimes (q4_0 / q4_k) to see memory/throughput tradeoffs across SKUs.
- Validate on additional cloud-region SKUs (some L40S offerings vary by region) to ensure driver availability.
- Run sustained 24h smoke tests to check for driver regressions or thermal throttling in long-running Dedicated capacity.

Notes to reviewers / context:
- This is a working note (internal) capturing a mix of experiment logs and early conclusions. Some numbers are averages over 3 runs; raw CSVs and nsys captures are attached in linked_artifacts/GITHUB-PR-987.
- If you are iterating on the bench scripts, please coordinate with Diego to avoid conflicting runs on the benchmarking pool.

Appendix: quick command snippets:
- Run a single GPU perf test:
  python scripts/bench/run_bench.py --model 7B --seq-in 128 --seq-out 256 --batch 16 --gpu 0 --cuda 12.0
- Profile with nsys:
  nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output bench_h100_12_0 ./bin/rdinfer --config bench/config-7b.yaml

End of doc.
